title: Finding my path in tech: What three terms as an Adtran co-op and intern taught me
summary: From software development and automation to machine learning, Joshua Reed’s experience as an Adtran co-op and intern gave him the opportunity to explore multiple technical disciplines while building the skills and confidence to shape his future career.
body_markdown:
When I stopped by the Adtran booth at the Auburn University career fair, I knew two things: I loved software development, and I had no clear idea what specific niche I wanted to build a career in. Cloud infrastructure? Cybersecurity? AI? Everything sounded interesting on paper, but I needed hands-on experience to figure it out.


The recruiting team made an immediate impression. Beyond being welcoming, they talked openly about the fact that Adtran had more than 20 distinct teams operating across the company. You were not locked into a single lane; you had room to explore. Being from Huntsville, Adtran was already a familiar name to me, and that flexibility made coming back home to work an easy decision.


**Day one: A familiar campus with a new lens**


I actually had memories of the Huntsville campus from when I was very young because my mom used to work at Adtran. Even so, stepping through the doors on day one as an adult engineer was an entirely different feeling. Adtran has a massive footprint, and the scale of the operation hits you right away. It was exciting, but definitely a little nerve-wracking.


What immediately broke the ice was the cohort. I started alongside roughly 20 other co-ops. While I grew up in the area, most of the other students were from outside Huntsville and eager to build a social circle outside the office. By the end of our first week, a group of us were out playing sand volleyball after work. Having that built-in peer group made the transition from college campus to corporate campus smooth and genuinely fun.


**Co-op vs. intern: Two great paths with different flavors**


Having completed two co-op rotations and one summer internship term, I often get asked about the difference between the two tracks. The technical expectations and support structure are identical across both programs. You’re treated like an engineer from day one. You get a dedicated mentor who checks in consistently, weekly 1-on-1s with your manager, and plenty of guidance when you run into architectural roadblocks.


The real difference lies in the rhythm and social ecosystem:


- **The co-op track (multi-term commitment)** : This is ideal if you want deep immersion and built-in community. Co-ops have an active calendar of events, including lunch-and-learns, planned social outings, and game nights hosted at the apartment complexes where many students stay. It makes forming close friendships almost automatic across multiple semesters.
- **The internship track (single-term focus)** : This reflects the day-to-day life of a full-time employee. You can attend social events, but the focus is streamlined around integrating directly with your engineering team and delivering a defined project during your term.


Both paths offer tremendous value. If you want multi-semester flexibility and an active student network, co-op. If you want a focused trial run of full-time life over a single term, intern.


> You’re treated like an engineer from day one.


**Owning projects and charting my own rotation**


One of my biggest milestones came from building an internal release management dashboard designed for product owners. I had to build a UI from scratch using modern web tools, which was something I had never tackled before.


Demoing that dashboard across different groups gave me wide exposure to team leads and decision-makers across the company. That visibility proved invaluable. Everyone at Adtran is generous with their time and eager to share domain knowledge. Because of that open-door culture, I was able to network directly with the manager of the intelligence functions team, pitch my interest and land my next placement working directly on machine learning models.


At Adtran, you’re not just assigned a desk and forgotten about. If you perform well and show initiative, there’s remarkable flexibility to pivot toward projects that align with your evolving interests.


**Setting the foundation for graduate school and beyond**


My rotations created a natural progression:


1. **Term 1** : Building automated testing workflows and backend infrastructure
2. **Term 2** : Layering AI-assisted development tools into automation pipelines and frontend dashboards
3. **Term 3** : Joining the intelligence functions team to train and evaluate data models directly


That progression clarified my long-term direction. It turned an abstract curiosity about artificial intelligence into tangible engineering experience, directly inspiring me to pursue my Master of Science in Data Science at Vanderbilt University. Graduating from Auburn with three full terms of real-world infrastructure and data experience gave my graduate applications a practical edge that classroom theory alone could never match.


Because Adtran invests heavily in hiring junior talent directly from its co-op and intern pools, your mentors and managers treat their guidance as a long-term investment rather than an afterthought.


**Final takeaway**


If you are considering a co-op or internship at Adtran, my advice is simple: **learn aggressively, ask questions without hesitation, and take advantage of the community around you** . The technical problems are challenging, the tools are modern, and the opportunity to steer your own career path is there if you take the initiative.
